subject: science

items.q: Steam from a kettle condenses into water on a cold window. What happens to energy as the steam condenses?
items.correct: The steam gives out energy to the window
items.misconception: The steam takes in energy from the window
items.why: Students may picture particles 'letting go' of energy as they break away, and a freezer needs electricity, which suggests that freezing takes energy in. Jasien (2013), summarised by the IOP's Spark research review, reports that many undergraduates could not correctly relate exothermic and endothermic processes to 'warm' and 'cold' in a study of freezing and boiling, but does not report this exact reversal. It is a common error teachers see. Particles need energy to move apart, so melting, boiling and evaporating take energy in. When particles come together in condensing and freezing, energy is given out; a freezer works by pumping that energy out of the food.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: No energy moves, as it is just water

items.q: Pure water is boiling in a pan, and the hob stays on. What happens to the water's temperature while it boils?
items.correct: It stays at its boiling point
items.misconception: It keeps rising as it is heated
items.why: Outside a change of state, heating does make the temperature rise, so students expect it always will. The IOP's Spark research review reports that many students think the temperature of boiling water will continue to rise if it is heated (citing Jasien, 2013, and Chu et al., 2012), and RSC Education ('Four simple experiments with counter-intuitive results') notes that students are likely to think temperature rises during melting or boiling. During melting or boiling, a pure substance stays at one temperature until the change is complete. The energy is changing the state, not raising the temperature.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: It falls as heat leaves in bubbles

items.q: The diagram shows the particles of a pure substance before and after a change of state. What must happen for this change to take place?
items.correct: Energy must be transferred to the substance
items.misconception: None is needed, as no new substance forms
items.why: Students meet energy changes mainly through burning and other reactions, and are taught that a change of state makes no new substance, so they decide nothing important happens to energy. It is a common error teachers see. Changes of state are physical changes, but they still transfer energy: in when solids melt and liquids boil, out when gases condense and liquids freeze.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: Energy must leave as the particles break free

items.q: The graph shows the temperature of a pure solid heated steadily. It melts between P and Q. What is true between P and Q?
items.correct: It takes in energy, which changes its state
items.misconception: It takes in no energy, as its temperature is steady
items.why: Students treat temperature and energy (heat) as the same thing, so no rise in temperature seems to mean no energy going in; this step is our inference from the research. The IOP's Spark research review reports that even able secondary students often cannot tell temperature and heat apart (Kesidou and Duit, 1993), and that many students struggle to explain why the temperature stays constant during a change of state despite continuous heating. Temperature and energy are different things. During melting and boiling, energy keeps going in but the temperature stays the same until the change is complete.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: It gives out energy, as its particles break away

items.q: On a cool, cloudy day a puddle slowly dries up. No heater or sunshine warms it. What happens to energy as the water evaporates?
items.correct: Energy is taken in from the surroundings
items.misconception: None is needed, as nothing hot is near it
items.why: Students link energy with visible heating, and a puddle drying on a cool day has no visible heat source. Paik (2015, Chemistry Education Research and Practice), who studied pupils in grades 4–6 (about 10–12 years old), notes that science textbooks show no example of evaporation with a visible heating source, and suggests that 'it might be difficult to realize that energy is needed when a liquid changes into a gas'. Every evaporation takes in energy. When nothing obvious heats the liquid, the energy comes from its surroundings, which is why evaporating sweat cools your skin.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: It is given out as the particles escape

items.q: Pure iron melts and freezes at 1538 °C. Liquid iron poured into a mould turns solid at this temperature. What happens to energy?
items.correct: It is given out to the mould and the air
items.misconception: None, as nothing can freeze when that hot
items.why: In everyday life freezing means ice, freezers and cold weather; the step from 'not freezing' to 'so no energy is given out' is our inference. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) concludes that the idea that freezing must occur at 'cold' temperatures seems to be firmly fixed in many students. Every substance has its own freezing (melting) point, and some are very hot. Whenever a liquid turns solid it is freezing, and it transfers energy to its surroundings.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.random_wrong: It is taken in from the mould and from the air

items.q: What happens in an endothermic reaction?
items.correct: Energy is taken in from the surroundings
items.misconception: Energy is given out to the surroundings
items.why: The two words sound alike and both end in '-thermic'. Jasien (2013, Journal of Chemical Education), summarised by the IOP's Spark research review, found that many first-year undergraduates could not correctly relate exothermic and endothermic processes to 'warm' and 'cold'. Exo = exit: energy goes out and the surroundings get warmer. Endo = into: energy goes in and the surroundings get colder.
items.random_wrong: Cold is given out to the surroundings

items.q: The diagram shows a thermometer in citric acid solution before and after adding sodium hydrogencarbonate (baking soda). What does it show about the reaction?
items.correct: Endothermic: it took in energy from the surroundings
items.misconception: Exothermic: the chemicals gave out their energy
items.why: Students do not separate the reacting chemicals from their surroundings (the water, beaker, thermometer and air); the consequence for thermometer readings described here is our inference. Jasien (2013), summarised by the IOP's Spark research review, reports that many first-year undergraduates had difficulty clearly distinguishing systems and surroundings. The thermometer measures the surroundings. If energy goes into the chemicals it comes out of the surroundings, so the temperature falls (endothermic); if energy comes out of the chemicals, the surroundings warm up (exothermic).
items.random_wrong: Endothermic: it gave cold out to the surroundings

items.q: Which of these is an endothermic chemical reaction?
items.correct: Heating calcium carbonate until it breaks down
items.misconception: Ice melting into water in a warm drink
items.why: Changes of state come with energy changes, and something visibly changes, as in a reaction. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Ahtee and Varjola's finding that around a fifth of students aged 13–14 and 17–18 thought dissolving and changes of state were chemical reactions. Ask whether a new substance is made. Ice, water and steam are all water, so melting, freezing and condensing are physical changes that take in or give out energy, not reactions.
items.random_wrong: A candle burning once a match lights it

items.q: A hand warmer contains iron powder. When it is opened, the iron reacts with oxygen in the air and the pack warms up. Which is correct?
items.correct: Exothermic: it transfers energy to your hands
items.misconception: Exothermic: it creates new energy from nothing
items.why: Everyday talk says fires 'make' heat and batteries 'run out'. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reviews research in which two-thirds of 15-year-olds, asked directly, said 'Energy is used up or lost' (Brook and Driver), and lists 'Energy can be created and used up' among students' key difficulties. Track where the energy goes. The total amount stays the same; it only moves between the chemicals and their surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Endothermic: it takes in energy and heats up

items.q: A gas fire needs a spark to light it. Then it keeps burning by itself and warms the room. What type of reaction is the burning?
items.correct: Exothermic: once lit, it gives energy to the room
items.misconception: Endothermic: it needs energy from a spark to start
items.why: Students see the match or spark going in and conclude that the reaction takes in heat. The Victorian Department of Education's Science Continuum P–10 ('Energy producing and consuming reactions') reports that many students consider examples like the burning of paper or a candle to be energy-consuming (endothermic) reactions. Ask what the reaction does once it is going. Burning gives out far more energy than the match supplied and keeps going by itself, so it is exothermic. A reaction is endothermic only if it takes in energy overall.
items.random_wrong: Exothermic: it passes on the spark's energy

items.q: Which of these is an exothermic chemical reaction?
items.misconception: Heating copper carbonate in a flame
items.why: The reactions students meet first, such as burning, give out energy. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) warns that pupils may come to think all reactions produce heat if the idea is taught too generally, but reports no study of it. It is a common error teachers see. Look at what the reaction does to its surroundings: a temperature rise means exothermic, a fall means endothermic. When you heat chemicals with a burner, the heat you feel comes from the burner, so it does not show that the reaction is exothermic: thermal decomposition, for example, takes energy in.
items.random_wrong: Steam condensing on a cold window

items.q: When something cools down, does 'cold' move into it?
items.correct: No. Cold is not a thing that moves. Something cools when energy is transferred out of it to colder surroundings; an endothermic reaction feels cold because it takes energy in from your hand.
items.misconception: Cold is a substance that flows: it moves from cold objects into things that cool, freeze or condense, and an endothermic reaction gives out cold.
items.why: Everyday language treats cold as a thing ('shut the door, you're letting the cold in'). The IOP's Spark research review reports that some students think of cold as an entity that behaves like heat, and that early secondary students often describe flows of 'coldness' (Schnittka and Bell, 2011); Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Osborne and Cosgrove's finding that pupils aged 12–17 explained water forming on the outside of a jar of ice with 'coldness comes through the glass'. Only energy is transferred, and it goes from the hotter object to the colder one. 'Getting cold' means losing energy; 'feeling cold' means energy is leaving your hand.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: What are the bubbles in boiling water made of?
items.correct: Water vapour (steam). The bubbles form when liquid water turns into a gas inside the liquid. Heat is not a substance, so it cannot make bubbles.
items.misconception: Heat is a kind of substance: the bubbles in boiling water are made of heat escaping from the water.
items.why: Everyday speech treats heat as stuff ('let the heat out', 'heat rises'). Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Osborne and Cosgrove's finding that 30% of 12-year-olds said the bubbles in boiling water were made of heat. Heat is energy being transferred, not a substance. The bubbles are water vapour, and while the water boils its temperature stays at the boiling point.
items.specStatementText: energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: When a fuel burns, does the energy given out come from the match or spark that lit it?
items.correct: No. The match or spark gives a tiny amount of energy to start the reaction. The large amount of energy given out comes from the fuel and oxygen as they react.
items.misconception: The energy given out when a fuel burns comes from the flame, match or spark used to light it.
items.why: The flame is the visible 'hot thing', so students credit it with the energy. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC) reports Barker's study in which some 16-year-olds, asked where the energy comes from when methane burns, answered 'from the flame'. The match or spark only starts the reaction. The energy transferred to the surroundings comes from the reacting fuel and oxygen, which is why a small spark can start a big fire.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented
